translation.text: In the second year of the reign of Darius, Haggai and Zechariah son of Iddo, the prophets, prophesied to the Jews who were in Judea[a] and Jerusalem in the name of the Lord God of Israel, to them[b].

footnotes.text: Or 'Judah' for 'Judea'; the Greek regional name is Ἰουδαία.
The closing ἐπ’ αὐτούς may also be understood as 'over them' or 'concerning them.' The main wording 'to them' is retained; the compressed phrase is not resolved by this source-import repair.

lexical_decisions.rationale: The temporal phrase is retained as 'In the second year'; connective δέ is carried by the narrative context.
βασιλεία here denotes kingship/reign rather than the abstract 'kingdom.' The genitive construction is most naturally rendered 'of the reign of Darius.'
The aorist verb is the standard term for prophetic activity. English 'prophesied' is both accurate and natural.

lexical_decisions.source_word: Ἀγγαῖος καὶ Ζαχαρίας ὁ τοῦ Ἐδδεὶν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Haggai and Zechariah son of Iddo
alternatives: Haggai and Zechariah the son of Iddin/Iddo
Haggai and Zechariah, son of Iddo
lexical_decisions.rationale: The singular patronymic most naturally modifies Zechariah. The existing English name form Iddo is retained; this repair does not adjudicate a separate Hebrew parallel.
The directly checked printed body has one article and identifies Haggai and Zechariah as the prophets. The modern duplicate article is not evidence of an ancient scribal variant.
With the verb of prophesying, the phrase can express the audience addressed. The existing 'to the Jews' is retained; alternative prepositional senses are not resolved by this import repair.

lexical_decisions.source_word: τοὺς ἐν τῇ Ἰουδαίᾳ καὶ Ἰερουσαλήμ
lexical_decisions.chosen: who were in Judea and Jerusalem
alternatives: who were in Judah and Jerusalem
lexical_decisions.rationale: The existing regional rendering Judea is retained for Ἰουδαία; Judah is a possible English alternative for the regional name. No separate Hebrew parallel is adjudicated here.

lexical_decisions.source_word: ἐπὶ τῷ ὀνόματι Κυρίου θεοῦ Ἰσραήλ
lexical_decisions.chosen: in the name of the Lord God of Israel
alternatives: by the name of the Lord God of Israel
under the name of the Lord, God of Israel
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase expresses prophetic authorization. The existing English 'in the name of' and the divine title Lord are retained.

The closing ἐπ’ αὐτούς is compressed and permits different construals. The existing main-text 'to them' is preserved, with over/concerning alternatives disclosed; this narrow source-import repair does not establish a preferred syntactic or source-priority judgment.

theological_decisions.issue: Rendering κύριος in a Jewish-scriptural context
theological_decisions.rationale: The checked Greek reads Κυρίου. The existing Lord rendering follows the project default for κύριος without a claim about a Hebrew divine-name form.

theological_decisions.issue: How to render the prophetic relation expressed by ἐπί
theological_decisions.chosen_reading: prophesied to the Jews ... to them
alternative_readings: prophesied concerning the Jews ... concerning them
prophesied to the Jews ... over them
theological_decisions.rationale: The main wording is retained, not newly preferred by this repair. The final prepositional phrase remains interpretively compressed; its alternatives are preserved in the note without relying on an unverified parallel.

1.routing_rationale: Current record 1 only. Preserve the main wording apart from marker placement; remove the false duplicated-article transmission note because the checked printed body has one οἱ. Qualify the closing phrase without a new preferred-reading judgment. Existing lexicon labels are inherited metadata, not fresh consultation claims.

translation.text: Let everything be known to our lord the king: when we came into the land of Judea and to Jerusalem, the city, we found the elders of the captivity of the Jews[a] in Jerusalem, the city, building a great new house for the Lord[b], with costly hewn stones, with timber laid in the buildings,

footnotes.text: Or, more literally, 'the elders of the Jews of the captivity.' The Greek wording is compressed; the sense is the leadership of the Jewish exile/returnee community.
'House for the Lord' refers to the temple.

alternatives: Be it known in every respect
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase is an epistolary/report formula. 'Let everything be known' preserves the imperative force of ἔστω with natural English while keeping the breadth of πάντα.

alternatives: to our sovereign lord the king
lexical_decisions.rationale: κύριος here is a courtly title for the Persian king, not a divine title. 'Lord' follows the project's default for κύριος and fits the deferential register; 'our lord the king' preserves both nouns.
The participle is temporal in context, introducing the circumstances of the report. 'When we came' is idiomatic and sufficiently close to the Greek.
χώρα can mean land, region, or territory. 'Land of Judea' is broad and avoids over-specifying an administrative nuance not explicit in the Greek.
The appositional wording is somewhat repetitive in Greek and is retained in a lightly smoothed form to reflect the source's emphasis.
In this context the verb means 'found/encountered' rather than 'seized.' The object is the elders engaged in building, so 'we found' best fits the sense.
The existing English retains the literal captivity wording in the compressed phrase identifying the Jewish elders; a smoother exilic-community alternative remains in the note.

alternatives: the elders of the Jews of the exile
the Jewish elders of the captivity
lexical_decisions.rationale: The elder/Jew wording is retained, with τῆς αἰχμαλωσίας represented as 'of the captivity' in the intervening English phrase. The note gives the alternative ordering without changing the main.
οἶκος literally means 'house.' Because the dative τῷ κυρίῳ marks it as God's house, 'house for the Lord' preserves the temple reference without importing 'temple' where the Greek says 'house.'
Here κύριος refers to Israel's God. Per doctrine, it is rendered 'Lord.' 'For the Lord' fits the construction with οἶκον in English.
Both adjectives modify οἶκον. 'Great new house' preserves both descriptors straightforwardly; 'magnificent' would over-interpret μέγαν.

λίθοι are stones; ξυστῶν here describes worked/dressed stone rather than raw fieldstone; πολυτελῶν adds the sense of costly or luxurious quality. 'Hewn stones' is natural English for worked building stone and stays close to the construction context.

alternatives: wood being set in the houses
lexical_decisions.rationale: ξύλων is best rendered 'timber/wood'; τιθεμένων is a participle meaning being placed or laid; οἴκοις in this construction refers to the building structures/rooms rather than domestic houses specifically. 'Timber laid in the buildings' preserves the construction imagery.

theological_decisions.issue: Rendering κύριος in one verse for both the Persian king and Israel's God
theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Use 'lord' for the kingly title in lowercase within the phrase 'our lord the king,' and 'Lord' for God in 'house for the Lord.'
alternative_readings: Use 'master' for the king and 'Lord' for God
theological_decisions.rationale: The Greek uses the same lexical item in two referents. English capitalization and context distinguish them without changing the underlying term. This preserves lexical transparency while avoiding confusion.
theological_decisions.doctrine_reference: DOCTRINE.md: κύριος default English 'Lord'; translate titles, preserve meaning

8.routing_rationale: Current 8 plus the stone-and-timber prefix of current 9, following the checked inline numeral 9 before καὶ τὰ ἔργα. Transfer only the two material lexical entries from 9. Keep the compressed-elders note with its actual phrase; keep the house note with Lord. The old note on diligence belongs in 9, not with the moved stones.

translation.text: and those works being done with diligence[a], and the work prospering in their hands, being completed with all glory[b] and care.

footnotes.text: Or 'with haste' for 'with diligence'; the Greek phrase ἐπὶ σπουδῆς can emphasize urgency as well as earnest care.
'Glory' here likely carries the sense of splendor or magnificence in the workmanship, not only honor in an abstract sense.

lexical_decisions.source_word: τὰ ἔργα ἐκεῖνα ἐπὶ σπουδῆς γινόμενα
lexical_decisions.chosen: those works being done with diligence
alternatives: those works being done with haste
those works being carried out earnestly
lexical_decisions.rationale: σπουδή can denote eagerness, diligence, earnestness, and in some contexts haste. In a royal building report, 'with diligence' best captures careful energetic execution without implying recklessness.

lexical_decisions.source_word: εὐοδούμενον τὸ ἔργον ἐν ταῖς χερσὶν αὐτῶν
lexical_decisions.chosen: the work prospering in their hands
alternatives: the work succeeding in their hands
the work advancing under their hands
lexical_decisions.rationale: εὐοδόω means to prosper or succeed. The idiom 'in their hands' is retained because it is transparent in English and reflects the source's agency idiom.

lexical_decisions.source_word: ἐν πάσῃ δόξῃ καὶ ἐπιμελείᾳ συντελούμενα
lexical_decisions.chosen: being completed with all glory and care
alternatives: being finished with every splendor and diligence
being brought to completion with full honor and carefulness
lexical_decisions.rationale: συντελούμενα means being completed or brought to completion. δόξα in this architectural context can suggest splendor/glory; ἐπιμέλεια is care, attention, diligence. 'With all glory and care' preserves the elevated tone while remaining readable.

9.routing_rationale: Retain current 9 after its stone-and-timber prefix moves to 8. Keep only the work/diligence/prospering/completion lexical entries. Reanchor a to diligence and b to glory; the main remaining wording is unchanged.

translation.text: Then we questioned these elders, saying, ‘Who commanded you to build this house[a] and lay the foundations of these works?’

footnotes.text: 'This house' refers to the temple in Jerusalem.

lexical_decisions.rationale: The imperfect/middle form conveys an act of asking for information. 'Questioned' fits the official investigative setting better than the softer 'asked,' while remaining natural English.
πρεσβύτεροι here refers to recognized community elders/leaders, not merely men advanced in age. 'Elders' preserves the social-political role.
The question asks whose command authorized the works; the existing main wording 'Who commanded you' is retained.
The finite Greek question is expressed in the existing English construction 'Who commanded you to build'; the restored second predicate is coordinated under the same construction.
οἶκος literally means 'house.' In this context it refers to the temple, but 'house' preserves the source wording and biblical idiom without over-specifying beyond the Greek.

lexical_decisions.chosen: lay the foundations of these works
lexical_decisions.rationale: The checked printed question includes this second foundation predicate before the next inline verse. English coordinates it with 'to build' under the retained authorization question. This is a translation of the restored printed clause, not a new lexicon consultation.

10.routing_rationale: Current 10 plus the previously omitted printed question tail τὰ ἔργα ταῦτα ἐθεμελιοῦτε;. The checked body does not end abruptly at and, so delete that false textual-variant note. Retain the house note and anchor it to house; no material transfers from 11.

translation.text: whose height is sixty cubits and width sixty cubits, with three courses of polished stone and one course of new local timber; and let the expense be given from the house of Cyrus the king.

lexical_decisions.rationale: The printed relative οὗ continues the house in 23. It does not describe fire; the duplicated sacrifice/fire fragment is removed from this unit while the complete wording in 23 remains untouched.

lexical_decisions.source_word: τὸ ὕψος πηχέων ἑξήκοντα, πλάτος πηχέων ἑξήκοντα
lexical_decisions.chosen: height is sixty cubits and width sixty cubits
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retain both existing dimensions and cubit units without harmonizing another account.

lexical_decisions.source_word: διὰ δόμων λιθίνων ξυστῶν τριῶν καὶ δόμου ξυλίνου ἐγχωρίου καινοῦ ἑνός
lexical_decisions.chosen: with three courses of polished stone and one course of new local timber
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retain the existing English building-material details and course counts. This bounded partition repair does not independently approve every lexical choice or claim a fresh lexicon consultation.

lexical_decisions.source_word: καὶ τὸ δαπάνημα δοθῆναι ἐκ τοῦ οἴκου Κύρου τοῦ βασιλέως
lexical_decisions.chosen: and let the expense be given from the house of Cyrus the king
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retain the existing expense clause and house wording without a separate semantic revision.

24.routing_rationale: Current 24 only after removing its duplicate sacrifice/fire fragment, already complete in untouched 23. Printed οὗ replaces the incorrect modern οὓ; whose attaches to the house in 23. Other English building details are retained. No pre-existing active lexical or theological entries were present in 24; the bounded entries here document retention and relative-clause routing, not full lexical approval.

translation.text: He also ordered Sisinnes, governor of Syria and Phoenicia, and Sathrabuzanes and their associates and the appointed governors in Syria and Phoenicia, to keep away from the place, but to leave Zerubbabel, the servant of the Lord and governor of Judea, and the elders of the Jews alone[a] to build that house of the Lord on the site.

footnotes.text: Or 'allow Zerubbabel ... and the elders of the Jews to build that house of the Lord on the site.' The Greek leave/permit verb is followed by an explicit building infinitive.

lexical_decisions.rationale: Aorist of προστάσσω denotes issuing an authoritative directive. 'Ordered' is clear modern English and preserves the force without sounding overly stiff.

In the construction προσετάξεν ... ἐπιμεληθῆναι, the infinitive expresses the content of the order. Rather than woodenly reproducing both verbs, English idiom is best served by folding the sense into 'ordered ... to,' while preserving the directive force.
The term denotes a provincial ruler/administrator. 'Governor' is the most natural and broadly intelligible equivalent in this context.
Here the word refers to administrative associates rather than intimate companions. 'Associates' fits the official setting and remains readable.
The participle ἀποτεταγμένοις conveys being assigned/appointed, and ἡγεμόσιν refers to rulers or governors. The combined rendering preserves both elements in natural English.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to keep away from the place
alternatives: to stay away from the place
to refrain from interfering with the place
lexical_decisions.rationale: Literally 'to keep away from the place.' In context the sense is noninterference with the temple site. 'Keep away from the place' preserves the spatial wording while implying official noninterference.
The keep-away directive is followed by ἐᾶσαι and an explicit building infinitive. The existing leave-alone wording is retained and completed by 'to build'; permit/allow remains a genuine alternative.

Although παῖς can mean child or servant, in a royal-administrative and honorific biblical context 'servant' is the established and contextually appropriate sense. κύριος is rendered 'Lord' per doctrine.
The term denotes one in authority over a region. 'Governor' matches the administrative context and aligns with ἐπάρχῳ without forcing an artificial distinction in English.
In Jewish communal context, 'elders' is the standard rendering and likely denotes recognized leaders rather than merely aged men.

lexical_decisions.source_word: τὸν οἶκον τοῦ κυρίου ἐκεῖνον οἰκοδομεῖν ἐπὶ τοῦ τόπου
lexical_decisions.chosen: to build that house of the Lord on the site
alternatives: to build that house of the Lord at the place
lexical_decisions.rationale: Restore the explicit printed building permission and its site phrase within the sentence governed by leave/permit. No separate source-priority judgment or new lexicon consultation is claimed.

theological_decisions.issue: Rendering of κύριος in the phrase παῖδα Κυρίου
theological_decisions.rationale: The project default renders κύριος as 'Lord.' In this Jewish-scriptural context it carries reverential weight and should not be flattened to 'master.'
The phrase is honorific and covenantal rather than biological. 'Servant of the Lord' preserves biblical idiom without importing messianic claims beyond the text.
theological_decisions.doctrine_reference: DOCTRINE.md: translate titles; preserve meaning and ambiguity

26.routing_rationale: Current 26 plus its omitted printed building-permission tail. Retain the other main wording and lexical choices; move the allow/leave alternative from Sisinnes to the actual leave-alone clause. The source addition is a modern import repair, not evidence of an ancient omission.

translation.text: so that libations[a] may be offered to God Most High for the king and his sons, and that they may pray for their lives[b].

footnotes.text: Greek singular 'life', referring to the king and his sons.

lexical_decisions.rationale: Introduces purpose; 'so that' is natural modern English while preserving the purposive force.
Passive/subjunctive sense fits the clause governed by ὅπως. 'Offered' is idiomatic for sacrificial context and matches cultic usage better than the more generic 'brought'.
The Greek specifically denotes drink offerings/libations. 'Libations' is slightly more formal but precise; 'drink offerings' is a valid alternative preserved as a lexical alternative.
This preserves both θεῷ and the epithet ὑψίστῳ. 'God Most High' is concise and natural in English, while retaining the title's theological weight.

lexical_decisions.source_word: ὑπὲρ τοῦ βασιλέως καὶ τῶν παίδων
lexical_decisions.chosen: for the king and his sons
alternatives: on behalf of the king and his children
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑπέρ here expresses benefit/intercession. παῖδες can mean children or sons; in royal context 'sons' is the more likely and more specific rendering, matching dynastic language.
Straightforward rendering of the subjunctive coordinated with the prior purpose clause.

The printed ζωῆς completes the phrase in this unit rather than opening 31. It explicitly supplies life, not an elliptical welfare object. Greek has the singular life; the English distributive plural refers to the king and his sons and is disclosed in the note.

theological_decisions.issue: Rendering the divine title ὁ ὕψιστος
theological_decisions.rationale: This is a title for Israel's God in a royal-imperial context. The chosen rendering preserves the title's meaning without importing later doctrinal nuance. Word order is adjusted for natural English while keeping both elements explicit.

30.routing_rationale: Current 30 plus the misplaced Greek ζωῆς from current 31. Neither old main English rendered that noun, so restore lives in the prayer rather than moving a nonexistent English prefix. Replace the stale elliptical-welfare decision and note with the now-complete Greek phrase; keep the libations alternative anchored to libations.

translation.text: And issue an order that if anyone transgresses any part of what has been written and nullifies it, a beam shall be taken from his own property and he shall be hanged on it[a], and his possessions shall become royal property.

footnotes.text: Or 'suspended on it'; 'impaled' is a possible contextual interpretation. The Greek hang/suspend wording does not specify the precise method.

lexical_decisions.rationale: The infinitive continues the administrative/jussive sequence and refers to an official royal directive. 'Issue an order' is natural modern English while preserving the formal governmental sense.
The verb denotes violating or going beyond what is prescribed. 'Transgresses' preserves the legal force better than a weaker 'disobeys,' though 'violates' is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: any part of what has been written
lexical_decisions.rationale: τι with the genitive plural naturally means 'anything/any part of the things written.' The rendering makes explicit that the reference is to the written decree without over-specifying beyond the Greek.
The verb expresses invalidation or cancellation. Match the existing main 'nullifies it', retaining the other legal renderings as alternatives.
ξύλον can denote wood, timber or a beam. Retain beam in this punitive property context without claiming verification of a separate parallel.
The Greek phrase broadly denotes what belongs to him. The existing main property wording is retained; the more specific house alternative is not established by this repair.
The Greek verb denotes hanging or suspension. Retain the main hanged wording; impaled is a possible contextual interpretation, not a method specified by this verb or newly established here.
The phrase refers to what belongs to him materially. 'Possessions' is clear modern English and broad enough to include all assets.
The adjective means belonging to the king/royal domain. 'Royal property' preserves the formal legal result of confiscation.

theological_decisions.issue: How specifically to render the penalty verb κρεμασθῆναι
alternative_readings: he shall be suspended on it
theological_decisions.rationale: Retain the direct hanging/suspension wording and disclose impalement as a possible contextual interpretation. The Greek verb does not establish the precise method, and this import repair supplies no new historical verification.
theological_decisions.doctrine_reference: Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it; consistency of key terms, or documented exception.

31.routing_rationale: Current 31 after its Greek ζωῆς transfers to 30. There is no old English life prefix to remove. Preserve all main penalty wording; anchor its execution-method note to hanged on it rather than nullifies it, and align stale chosen fields with the actual English without an unverified parallel or historical-method claim.
